burrito-bowl-beef-or-pork-with-beans.title: Burrito Bowl, Beef or Pork, with Beans

content.title: About
content.content: A burrito bowl is a Mexican‑inspired dish served in a bowl with rice, choice of meat (beef or pork), beans, fresh vegetables, salsa and sour cream. It can be served cold or lightly warmed, making it a convenient fast‑food option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The bowl version was created as a lighter alternative to the traditional wrapped burrito.
Beef is often marinated steak, while pork usually comes from slow‑cooked shoulder.
Beans are typically black or pinto, both high in protein and fiber.
In the United States the dish is popular in fast‑casual chains as well as home kitchens.
The combination of rice, beans, and meat provides a complete amino‑acid profile.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Beef and pork supply high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Fiber from beans
items.content: Beans add soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice offers slow‑release energy, helping to keep you full longer.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and legumes provide B6, B12 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish contains iron, zinc and magnesium, which aid immunity and muscle function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beans.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salsa and sauces can be salty; people with hypertension should watch portions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Rice, meat and sauces make the bowl energy‑dense; portion control is advised for weight management.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: Meat must be fully cooked to avoid salmonella or campylobacter risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat the burrito bowl with a spoon, mixing all components together. Add guacamole, fresh cilantro, lime juice or hot sauce to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared bowl in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat the rice and meat if you prefer a warm meal.

chicken-drumstick-baked-coated-skin-coat.title: Chicken drumstick, baked, coated, skin/coating eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken drumsticks are the lower part of the thigh, containing meat, skin and a small bone. When baked in the oven with a coating, the skin becomes crispy while the meat stays juicy. This preparation is popular in many world cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Drumsticks are often used in dishes where juiciness and flavor are key, such as barbecues or casseroles.
Baking with a coating creates a crunchy crust without the need for large amounts of oil.
Chicken skin is rich in collagen, which turns into gelatin during cooking and supports joint health.
In some countries drumsticks are served with barbecue sauce, in others with spicy rubs.
Drumsticks are a more affordable source of protein compared with breast fillets.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken drumsticks provide complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: They contain B3 (niacin) and B6, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Iron, zinc and phosphorus in the meat support blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Skin supplies collagen
items.content: Eating the skin adds extra collagen, beneficial for skin and joints.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Drumsticks have virtually no carbs, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Drumsticks contain more fat than breast meat, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Undercooking risk
items.content: Improper cooking can leave meat undercooked, increasing the risk of foodborne illness.

items.title: Salt in coating
items.content: Pre‑made coatings often contain high sodium; choose low‑salt versions if you have hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken drumsticks can be served as a main dish, sliced for salads, added to soups, or used in sandwiches. The skin and coating are eaten together, providing crunch and flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh drumsticks in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen drumsticks last up to 9 months in the freezer. Before cooking, check for off‑odors or discoloration; discard if any are present.

content.title: About
content.content: A jelly‑filled doughnut is a sweet, ring‑shaped pastry glazed on the outside and stuffed with fruit jelly. The dough is typically made from wheat flour, sugar, eggs, milk and yeast, while the jelly can be strawberry, raspberry, apricot or other berry preserves.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Doughnuts appeared in Europe in the 19th century and quickly became popular in the United States.
The classic American “jelly‑filled doughnut” is often called a “Boston cream” only when the filling is custard, not jelly.
Japan has a similar treat called “anpan,” but it usually lacks a glaze.
There are over 100 filling varieties, ranging from traditional fruit jams to chocolate and caramel creams.
Doughnuts are commonly served for breakfast, as a dessert, or as a street snack.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Doughnuts provide a quick boost of energy due to their carbohydrate content, which can be useful before physical activity.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The yeast‑based dough and eggs supply B1, B2 and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants in the jelly
items.content: Fruit jelly contains vitamin C and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Trans and saturated fats
items.content: If the dough is prepared with margarine or a lot of butter, the pastry may contain unhealthy fats.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Doughnuts may contain gluten, eggs, milk and nuts, which is important for people with food allergies.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Jelly‑filled doughnuts are usually eaten fresh; they can be warmed briefly in a microwave. They are convenient as a grab‑and‑go snack or served alongside coffee or tea.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator, though they may become less soft.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg white is the clear liquid surrounding the yolk. It is rich in protein, virtually free of fat and carbohydrates, and contains small amounts of B‑vitamins and minerals such as selenium and potassium. Egg white is widely used to make omelets, scrambled eggs, or fried dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is about 90 % water and 10 % protein.
It contains all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.
When whipped, egg white forms a stable foam, ideal for meringues and soufflés.
Selenium in egg white supports antioxidant protection in the body.
Egg white is a staple in many diet plans because of its low calorie content.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: One large egg white provides roughly 3.6 g of protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Very low in fat
items.content: Egg white contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in selenium
items.content: Selenium helps maintain immune function and protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: A single egg white has about 17 kcal, useful for weight‑management regimes.

items.title: Heart‑friendly
items.content: Absence of cholesterol in egg white makes it safe for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Biotin binding
items.content: Raw egg whites contain avidin, which can bind biotin and lead to deficiency if consumed in excess.

items.title: Salmonella risk
items.content: Improper storage or undercooking can allow salmonella contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Egg whites can be prepared as an omelet, scrambled, or simply fried. For an omelet, whisk the whites with a pinch of salt, pour into a hot pan, and cook until set and lightly golden. Scrambled egg whites are cooked while continuously stirring until curds form. Fried egg whites are common in Asian cuisine, often seasoned with soy sauce and mixed with vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store egg whites in a sealed container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Frozen egg whites keep for up to 6 months; thaw them in the fridge before use.

pizza-with-cheese-and-extra-vegetables-t.title: Pizza with cheese and extra vegetables, thick crust

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with cheese and extra vegetables on a thick crust is a flavorful dish that combines melted cheese, fresh vegetables (such as bell pepper, tomato, onion, mushrooms) and a hearty, dense dough. Perfect as a filling lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thick crust requires longer baking, resulting in a denser, more aromatic base.
The cheese blend often includes mozzarella and cheddar for optimal stretch and flavor.
Extra vegetables boost vitamin and fiber content, making the pizza more nutritious.
Traditional Italian pizza usually has a thin crust, but many countries favor thicker versions.
Pizza is commonly served with a tomato sauce made from fresh tomatoes and basil.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheese provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Vitamins from vegetables
items.content: Vegetables add vitamin C, vitamin A, and folate, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The dough and cheese supply complex carbs and protein for lasting satiety.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and peppers contain lycopene and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and whole‑grain dough (if used) increase fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Thick crust and cheese make the pizza calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Cheese and sauce can be high in sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The dough contains gluten, so the pizza is unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, sliced into wedges. Add fresh herbs (basil, oregano) or a drizzle of olive oil if desired. Pair with a light salad for balance.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore crust crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Rum is a distilled spirit made from fermented sugarcane juice or molasses. Diet cola is a calorie‑free soft drink sweetened with artificial sweeteners instead of sugar. The combination is popular in cocktails such as a “Rum‑Cola,” offering a flavorful drink with reduced sugar content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rum has a long history dating back to the 17th century, originating in the Caribbean.
Diet cola was first introduced in the 1960s as a response to growing demand for low‑calorie beverages.
The rum‑and‑cola mix became popular in the United States during the 1970s and serves as a base for many bar recipes.
Some countries offer caffeine‑free diet cola, while others include caffeine.
Rum can be light (white) or aged (dark); each type imparts a distinct flavor profile to the cocktail.

items.title: Moderate consumption may promote relaxation
items.content: Small amounts of alcohol have a calming effect, helping to reduce stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie, sugar‑free option
items.content: Diet cola contains no sugar, lowering the overall calorie count compared with regular cola.

items.title: Antioxidants in aged rum
items.content: Aged rum contains trace amounts of polyphenols, which can provide antioxidant benefits.

items.title: Alcohol‑related risks
items.content: Excessive rum consumption can lead to dependence, liver damage, and other health issues.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to the artificial sweeteners used in diet cola.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of certain medications; consult a healthcare professional if needed.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Combine 50 ml of rum with 150–200 ml of diet cola in a glass over ice. Optionally add a lime wedge or a sprig of mint for extra aroma. Serve immediately while cold.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store rum in a cool, dark place in a tightly sealed bottle for several years. Keep opened diet cola refrigerated to maintain freshness and carbonation.
